name: Brownish Yellow
lede: Brownish yellow is the old descriptive term for a dull, deep yellow, the family of ochre and mustard, and in 1751 one fashionable shade of it was called caca dauphin.

sections.title: A description, not a pigment
sections.body: Brownish yellow is how the books describe a yellow pulled toward brown, from mustard to ochre to an unglazed clay tile [1][2]. Paterson glosses *mustard brown* as a deep brownish-yellow and also uses the phrase for brick or flowerpot clay [1]. Pastoureau notes that the yellow earth pigments, the ochers, ran from bright yellow to light brownish yellow [3]. Compare [[mustard]], [[ochre]], [[gold]] and [[yellow]].

sections.title: Caca dauphin
sections.body: Pastoureau reports that in the last weeks of 1751 a brownish yellow was the court's fashion to celebrate the birth of the Duke of Burgundy, grandson of Louis XV, and was called caca dauphin, "dauphin dung" [4]. The shade spread from court to town, and today we would call it mustard, or in French caca d'oie [4]. He uses it as an example of how quickly new dyeing shades came and went in the eighteenth century [4].

sections.title: Where it turns up in materials
sections.body: The Pigment Compendium lists brownish yellow as the color of catechu brown mordanted with tin [5]. It also gives it for the impure lead mineral phosgenite, and for one stage of the heat tarnish on a metal powder [5][6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is rare in the archive: 27 of 23,781 paintings contain it, as photographed [7]. Almost all of it is highlight, 93 percent, which fits a yellow [7]. Among the paintings that hold it are Cornelis van Assendelft's *Shepherd with Sheep* of 1900 and Paul Sérusier's *Le Talisman* of 1888 [7].
